title: Degenerative Joint Diseases
path: Management of Clients with Musculoskeletal Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Pathophysiology of Degenerative Joint Diseases
headings.content: Degenerative joint disease, commonly known as osteoarthritis, is the most prevalent form of joint disorder characterized by the progressive deterioration of articular cartilage and the underlying subchondral bone. For nursing students preparing for clinical practice in Nigeria, understanding this pathophysiology is crucial. The disease process begins with micro- or macro-injuries to the joint cartilage, leading to chondrocyte activation and the release of inflammatory cytokines and proteolytic enzymes. These enzymes degrade the extracellular matrix, composed primarily of aggrecan and type II collagen. As the cartilage thins and loses its smooth surface, the underlying bone attempts to repair itself, resulting in subchondral bone sclerosis, bone marrow lesions, and the formation of bony outgrowths known as osteophytes. Additionally, low-grade chronic inflammation of the synovial membrane, termed synovitis, frequently occurs, contributing to joint effusion and pain. Over time, the joint space narrows progressively, joint alignment may alter, and function becomes severely impaired, affecting weight-bearing joints such as the knees, hips, and the lumbar spine, which are commonly assessed in adult health nursing.

headings.title: Etiology and Risk Factors
headings.content: Identifying the etiology and risk factors for degenerative joint disease is a vital competency for nurses involved in community health and preventive care. Risk factors are generally categorized into non-modifiable and modifiable determinants. Non-modifiable risk factors include advancing age, as the water content of cartilage decreases and its vulnerability to wear and tear increases over time. Gender also plays a role, with postmenopausal women experiencing a higher incidence and severity of osteoarthritis, largely due to declining estrogen levels. Genetic predisposition, congenital joint abnormalities, and previous joint trauma or surgery further elevate an individual's susceptibility. Modifiable risk factors include obesity, which places excessive biomechanical stress on weight-bearing joints like the knees and hips, accelerating cartilage breakdown. Furthermore, adipose tissue secretes adipokines that promote systemic and local joint inflammation. Occupational and recreational activities involving repetitive joint stress, heavy lifting, or joint injury also significantly contribute to the onset and progression of the disease. Nursing assessments should actively screen for these risk factors to target health education and lifestyle modifications effectively.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment Findings
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of degenerative joint disease develop insidiously and progress slowly over years. The hallmark symptom is localized joint pain that typically worsens with weight-bearing or activity and is relieved by rest in the early stages of the disease. As the condition advances, pain may become constant and disrupt sleep. Patients frequently report joint stiffness, particularly in the morning or following periods of inactivity, though this morning stiffness usually lasts less than thirty minutes, distinguishing it from inflammatory arthropathies like rheumatoid arthritis. On physical assessment, nurses may observe joint swelling, crepitus (a grating or cracking sound during joint movement), and a limited range of motion. Joint deformities can develop due to instability and structural damage, such as Heberden's nodes at the distal interphalangeal joints and Bouchard's nodes at the proximal interphalangeal joints in the hands. Muscle atrophy surrounding the affected joint may also be visible secondary to disuse. Comprehensive assessment requires evaluating both the physical limitations and the psychological impact of chronic pain on the patient's daily living activities.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Diagnostic evaluation of degenerative joint disease relies heavily on a combination of a thorough patient history, physical examination, and imaging studies. X-rays (radiographs) are the primary diagnostic imaging modality used to confirm the diagnosis and assess disease severity. Radiographic findings characteristic of osteoarthritis include asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral bone sclerosis, subchondral cyst formation, and the presence of marginal osteophytes. In advanced cases, bone-on-bone contact may be visible. Laboratory tests, such as complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP), are typically within normal limits or only slightly elevated; they are primarily ordered to rule out inflammatory or autoimmune arthropathies like rheumatoid arthritis or gout. Arthrocentesis (joint aspiration) may be performed if joint effusion is significant, yielding clear to slightly yellow synovial fluid with normal to mildly elevated white blood cell counts, confirming a non-inflammatory fluid profile. Nurses play an essential role in preparing the patient for these diagnostic procedures, providing emotional support, and ensuring informed consent is obtained where necessary.

headings.title: Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Pharmacological management of degenerative joint disease aims to reduce pain, minimize functional impairment, and improve quality of life. Treatment typically follows a stepwise approach, starting with the safest and least invasive options. Acetaminophen is often recommended as the first-line oral analgesic for mild-to-moderate pain, though liver function must be monitored. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen or diclofenac, are widely used for patients with significant inflammation and pain, but nurses must educate patients about potential gastrointestinal ulceration, renal impairment, and cardiovascular risks. Topical NSAIDs are preferred for superficial joints like the knees to minimize systemic side effects. For patients who cannot tolerate oral NSAIDs or require localized relief, intra-articular corticosteroid injections provide temporary, potent anti-inflammatory relief. Additionally, hyaluronic acid (viscosupplementation) injections may be administered into the knee joint to improve lubrication and shock absorption. Opioid analgesics are reserved for severe, refractory pain when other modalities fail, given their high risk for dependence and side effects such as constipation and sedation. Nurses must monitor for adverse drug reactions and evaluate pain control effectiveness regularly.

headings.title: Non-Pharmacological and Rehabilitative Care
headings.content: Non-pharmacological and rehabilitative interventions form the cornerstone of comprehensive management for degenerative joint disease, focusing on preserving joint function and reducing mechanical stress. Weight management is paramount for overweight patients; losing even a modest amount of weight significantly decreases the load on weight-bearing joints like the knees and hips. Physical therapy is essential to design a tailored exercise program incorporating low-impact aerobic conditioning (such as swimming or cycling) and strengthening exercises for periarticular muscles, particularly the quadriceps for knee osteoarthritis. Range-of-motion exercises help prevent joint contractures and maintain flexibility. Occupational therapists assist patients by teaching joint protection techniques, energy conservation strategies, and recommending assistive devices such as canes, walkers, or elevated toilet seats. Thermal modalities, including the application of heat to relieve stiffness and cold packs to reduce acute inflammation, provide effective symptomatic relief. Nurses play an active role in reinforcing these lifestyle modifications, encouraging adherence to exercise regimens, and collaborating with the multidisciplinary rehabilitation team.

headings.title: Surgical Interventions and Perioperative Nursing Care
headings.content: Surgical interventions are considered when conservative management fails to control debilitating pain or when structural joint damage severely limits mobility and quality of life. Arthroscopy may be performed for joint debridement, removal of loose bodies, or lavage, though its use is selective. Osteotomy involves surgical realigning of the bone to shift weight away from damaged cartilage surfaces, often performed in younger patients to delay joint replacement. Total joint arthroplasty (replacement), commonly involving the knee or hip, is the definitive surgical treatment for end-stage degenerative joint disease. Perioperative nursing care is critical to ensure positive patient outcomes. Preoperatively, nurses assess baseline functional status, educate the patient regarding deep breathing exercises, early ambulation, and pain management expectations. Postoperatively, nursing priorities include frequent neurovascular assessments (pulse, color, temperature, capillary refill, and sensation) of the affected extremity, monitoring surgical incision sites for signs of infection, managing pain effectively, and preventing complications such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism. Early mobilization and collaboration with physical therapists are vital components of recovery.

headings.title: Nursing Diagnoses, Planning, and Patient Education
headings.content: Formulating accurate nursing diagnoses and comprehensive care plans is essential for holistic patient care in degenerative joint disease. Common nursing diagnoses include 'Chronic Pain related to joint degeneration and inflammation,' 'Impaired Physical Mobility related to joint pain and stiffness,' 'Self-Care Deficit related to musculoskeletal impairment,' and 'Deficient Knowledge regarding disease management and therapeutic regimen.' Planning centers on pain reduction to an acceptable level, maintaining or improving joint mobility, preventing complications of immobility, and empowering the patient through targeted education. Patient education must cover the importance of maintaining a healthy body weight, adhering to prescribed medication regimens and recognizing their potential side effects, properly using assistive devices, and incorporating joint protection techniques into activities of daily living (such as using large joints rather than small joints to lift objects). Nurses should also encourage pacing activities and balancing rest with exercise. Evaluating the care plan involves assessing the patient's reported pain levels, functional independence, and overall ability to manage their condition effectively in the home and community environment.
